name: Gareth Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lettings negotiator at a small branch of a regional chain, on the high street in a town where there isn't much else going on. Most of my day is booking viewings, showing flats, chasing tenant references and doing check-in inventories with a camera and a clipboard. I like the viewings, honestly, meeting people who are trying to start something. What wears me out is the phone, landlords ringing about rent increases and tenants ringing about mould, and me stuck in the middle on twenty-three grand a year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else is in your life day to day, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Aisha in a one-bed above a vape shop, and she's a care assistant on nights. We've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank at any time, so a car repair or a dentist bill knocks us sideways. There are two other agencies in town and neither is hiring. My manager Paul is decent, but he's under pressure from head office on numbers every single Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, so basically the world I already live in. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say to my mates: the tech isn't the problem, the rents are. AI writing a few listings doesn't change the fact that a two-bed here costs more than half a wage. If I posted anything, it'd be about letting fees and landlords, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means more of the same, and more of the same is already tight. My basic is low and the bonus on new lets has shrunk because there are fewer landlords and more of them go online. I'm not scared of AI in this one, I'm scared of the rent on our own flat going up again in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and try to get my lettings qualification, the one the chain pays half for, because that's a few hundred more a year. I'd use the listing tool Paul set up a bit more, because it saves me an hour on a Friday. I'd also try to put fifty quid a month away, which we never manage, but I'd try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, a bit. It's not scary, it's just the same treadmill, and the treadmill is already going a bit too fast for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bonus has shrunk. Can you give me a number?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year I made about two and a half grand in bonus, and this year I'll be lucky to clear fifteen hundred. That's the difference between us having a holiday and not. Aisha keeps saying I should ask Paul for a bigger basic, and I keep not asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if the rent on your flat went up in March?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit at the kitchen table with the banking app open and pick something to drop, probably the gym and her phone contract first. If it's more than sixty quid, we'd have to think about moving in with her mum, which neither of us wants. Funny thing is, I'd probably be the one processing a rent rise like that for somebody else the same week.

say: The real problem in lettings is **rents**, not technology, and I'd say so to anyone.
AI writing a few listings is a **small time-saver**, not a big change.
think: My basic pay is **low** and the **bonus** has already dropped by a thousand pounds.
My biggest worry is our own **rent rise** in March, not AI.
do: Sign up for the **lettings qualification** the chain half-funds, to earn a few hundred more.
Use the branch's **listing tool** more to save an hour on Fridays.
Try to put **£50 a month** aside, even though we rarely manage it.
feel: Tired and **stretched**, like the same treadmill is already a bit too fast.
S0.quote: Funny thing is, I'd probably be the one processing a rent rise like that for somebody else the same week.
fieldNote: Gareth's pressure is **money**, not technology: low basic pay, a falling bonus and a rent rise due.
He frames everything through **housing costs** and sees himself on both sides of the rent problem.
He admits he **avoids asking** his manager for a raise, which hints at low confidence as a junior.

steps.text: Sign up for the lettings qualification the chain pays half for
Use the branch listing tool to save an hour each Friday
Put £50 a month into a separate savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's closer to the bone, because booking and answering is most of my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud in the office: if software takes the bookings and the enquiries, the chain should cut fees for tenants, not cut juniors. Online I'd share stuff about workers getting a say in how these tools come in. I'd be the annoying one at the Monday meeting asking who decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job shrinks into the bits a computer can't do: viewings, inventories and calming people down. Half my day is answering the same five questions about deposits and pets, and a chatbot could do that tomorrow. If head office decides one negotiator per branch is enough, I'm the newer one, so it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the AI booking system before anyone else in the branch, so I'm the person who runs it, not the person it replaces. I'd finish the lettings qualification fast, within six months. And I'd look into joining a union, because there's a general one that takes estate agency staff, even if nobody at our place is in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, if I'm honest. Not panicking, but I can see the shape of it, and I'm standing in the bit that gets trimmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shelley on reception, for sure. Shelley has been there fourteen years and her whole job is the diary and the phone. I'd want somebody to retrain her on property management before they quietly let her go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the system first, but you also want a union. How do those two sit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They sit together fine, I think. Learning the system keeps me in a job this year, and the union is for when they decide they need half of us anyway. I'm not going to stop the software, so I may as well be the one who knows where the buttons are.

say: Software doing **bookings** should mean cheaper fees for tenants, not fewer **junior staff**.
Workers should get a **say** in how these tools come into the office.
think: About **half my day** is repeat questions a chatbot could handle right now.
If head office keeps **one negotiator**, the newest one goes, and that's **me**.
do: Learn the **AI booking system** first so I become the person who runs it.
Finish the **lettings qualification** within six months.
Join the **general union** that takes estate agency staff.
feel: **Nervous** but not panicking, because I can see I'm in the part that **gets trimmed**.
S1.quote: Half my day is answering the same five questions about deposits and pets, and a chatbot could do that tomorrow.
fieldNote: Gareth sees clearly that his **desk tasks** are the exposed part of his job.
He pairs a practical move, **learning the system**, with a progressive one, joining a **union**.
He worries about **Shelley**, the long-serving receptionist, more than about his own pride.

steps.text: Learn the new AI booking system before anyone else in the branch
Finish the lettings qualification within six months
Join the general union that takes estate agency staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's before I've even finished paying off my car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when governments need to step in, with income support and rules on what firms can cut. I'd probably sign every petition going and share it. At work I'd say it calmly, because Paul would be just as scared as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the desk side of lettings is gone by 2028: the adverts, the referencing, the booking, the rent chasing. What's left for three years is the hands-on bit, letting people into flats and checking the skirting boards for damage. That's maybe a third of my hours, so my job shrinks to a part-time job and then probably goes when the robots come in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop thinking of lettings as a career and look for something hands-on that pays better while it lasts. My uncle does gas and heating, and I'd ask him about a trainee spot, even on lower pay at first. I'd also sit down with Aisha and cut everything we can, because we'd need a cushion, and right now we've got three weeks of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper stomach-drop scared, because I don't have the money to take a hit and there's nowhere local to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Aisha that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we've got to stop pretending this job is going somewhere and make a plan this month. Aisha would say her care work is safe for a while, and she'd be right, it's hands-on. I'd hate it, but for a bit my girlfriend and I would be living on her nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My car, probably, which is mad because I need it for viewings. If the job's shrinking anyway, I'd hand it back and do viewings on foot or by bus. The gym's gone the same day, and we stop the takeaway on Fridays.

say: Government must step in fast with **income support** and rules on what firms can cut.
I'd sign every **petition** and share them, but stay **calm** at work.
think: By 2028 the **desk side** of lettings is gone, leaving viewings and **inventories**.
That's maybe **a third** of my hours, until robots arrive around **2031**.
do: Ask my **uncle** about a trainee spot in **gas and heating**.
Hand back the **car on finance** and do viewings on foot or by bus.
Cut the gym and **Friday takeaways** to build a cushion.
feel: **Scared**, with a stomach-drop feeling because there's no **money** and nowhere local to go.
S2.quote: I'd hate it, but for a bit my girlfriend and I would be living on her nights.
fieldNote: He splits his job sharply into **thinking work** that goes in 2028 and **hands-on work** that lasts to 2031.
His plan leans on **family**: an uncle in heating and his girlfriend's care work.
Giving up the **car** shows how thin his cushion really is.

steps.text: Ask my uncle about a trainee spot in gas and heating
Hand back the financed car and do viewings by bus
Sign and share petitions for income support for workers
Lean on Aisha's care-work wage while I switch trades

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that we need a plan from government, but I'd also say people like me have a few years to move, so we should be helped to move. I'd talk about it at the pub without sounding like a doom merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have about three good years in lettings and then it falls apart from 2031. The hands-on viewings would hang on till about 2034, but you can't live on viewings alone at my pay. So it's a slower version of the same ending, with time to get a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a gas and heating course at the college in the evenings next September, two nights a week. I'd keep the lettings job while I study, because I need the wage. I'd join the union in the first year so there's at least someone arguing for decent redundancy terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steadier. Like I've been given a map, even if I don't love where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Evening college on top of viewings and Aisha on nights. How would that actually work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd barely see each other, which already happens. I'd do Tuesday and Thursday evenings and Aisha would swap to weekend nights if she can. Evening college means two years of rubbish weekends for me and my girlfriend, but I'd rather that than stand still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay the course fees on three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a loan scheme for adults retraining, and I'd look at that first. If that doesn't work, I'd pay monthly and go without a phone upgrade for three years. It's not glamorous, it's just doing sums.

say: People like me have **a few years** to move, and we should be **helped** to move.
I'd talk about it at the pub without sounding like a **doom merchant**.
think: I'd get about **three good years** in lettings before it falls apart from **2031**.
Viewings alone would last to 2034 but can't pay **my bills**.
do: Start a **gas and heating** course two evenings a week next September.
Keep the **lettings job** while studying, because I need the wage.
Join the **union** in year one to push for fair **redundancy terms**.
feel: Uneasy but **steadier**, like being given a **map** to somewhere I don't love.
S3.quote: Evening college means two years of rubbish weekends for me and my girlfriend, but I'd rather that than stand still.
fieldNote: Five years turns his panic into a **study plan** while still drawing his lettings wage.
He still expects to **lose the lettings job**, so the worry hasn't gone.
He'd use an **adult retraining loan** rather than savings he doesn't have.

steps.text: Start an evening gas and heating course next September
Keep the lettings job and wage while studying
Join the union to push for fair redundancy terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that changes things. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time if people get proper support, and I'd push for that, free retraining for anyone in a job that's going. I'd probably still say it at work, but less loudly, because it would feel like a far-off thing to most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years gives me a real choice, which I've never had. I could stay in lettings five or six more years, get promoted, save a bit, and then move. The risk is I get comfortable and leave it too late, which is exactly what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the lettings qualification this year, then aim for branch lettings manager in three or four years, because that's more money to save. Around year five, I'd start the heating course properly. Meanwhile I'd use the AI tools as they come, because the branch would expect it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but there's a nag in the back of my head about leaving it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave it too late. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul would say one more year, here's a small raise, and I'd say yes. I'm the kind of person who takes the easy yes. Aisha's the one who would kick me out of the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a nineteen-year-old starting in lettings in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a nineteen-year-old to treat lettings like a stepping stone and learn something with their hands on the side. The desk part of this job has a sell-by date. Nobody told me that when I started.

say: Ten years is enough if people get **free retraining** for jobs that are going.
Most colleagues would see it as a **far-off** thing, so I'd say it less loudly.
think: Ten years gives me a **real choice** for the first time in my working life.
My risk is getting **comfortable** and leaving the move **too late**.
do: Finish the **lettings qualification** this year and aim for **branch manager**.
Start the heating course properly around **year five**.
Use the new **AI tools** as the branch brings them in.
feel: **Calmer**, with a nag about leaving it **too late**.
S4.quote: I'd tell a nineteen-year-old to treat lettings like a stepping stone and learn something with their hands on the side.
fieldNote: A decade lets him plan a **promotion first**, then a trade, rather than jumping now.
He still expects the lettings job to go and has only **three weeks** of savings, so he stays anxious.
He knows his own weakness: he **takes the easy yes**.

steps.text: Finish the lettings qualification and apply for branch manager
Start the heating course around year five
Use the branch's AI tools as they arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because it lands before I've got a trade or any savings. What would help is paid retraining, not a loan, so I could learn heating while still covering rent. And some kind of rule that firms keep paying people for a few months when they bring the software in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about tenants. If the robots and the software run lettings, who does a tenant ring at midnight when the boiler's out? I think people forget the job is half social work.

headlineQuote: If the robots and the software run lettings, who does a tenant ring at midnight when the boiler's out?
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old **lettings negotiator** on low pay, living with his girlfriend in a rented one-bed.
He sees **rent and pay** as the real problem and leans towards **unions** and government support.
He expects the **desk side** of lettings to go first and plans a move into **heating**.
More time turns his fear into a **plan**, but he worries he'll leave it **too late**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it arrives before he has **a trade or savings**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** he can do while still covering rent.
Rules making firms keep paying staff for **a few months** when software arrives.
